# February 20, 1952

You arrived on a Wednesday, in the cold heart of a winter that the world was still sorting out.

---

## The World in Mid-Stride

Seven years had passed since the end of the most destructive war in human history, but the rebuilding was still very much underway. Europe was rising from rubble. The United States had settled into something new and uneasy: prosperity at home, anxiety abroad. A war was being fought in Korea — not won, not lost, grinding toward a stalemate that would take another eighteen months to freeze in place. The phrase *Cold War* was already in common use.

This was the world you entered: not peaceful, but hopeful. Not certain, but energetic.

---

## The Oslo Games

On the very day you were born, the **1952 Winter Olympics** were in their seventh day in Oslo, Norway. The Games ran February 14–25, and February 20 fell in the heart of the competition. Oslo had lobbied for these Games partly as a symbol of Norwegian recovery from Nazi occupation — a country reclaiming its identity through sport, on home snow. Speed skating, ski jumping, alpine events: the Norwegians dominated, and the world watched. You came into this world during the Games, which is a fine way to arrive.

---

## A Newborn's First Fear

Here is something parents in 1952 knew that their counterparts a decade later would not: genuine, daily terror of **polio**. The year you were born became the worst polio year in American history, with nearly 58,000 cases reported, thousands paralyzed, hundreds dead. Iron lungs hummed in hospital wards. Parents kept children away from public pools in summer. The Salk vaccine would not be approved until 1955 — three years away. You were born into a world that still had no reliable answer to a virus that could take a healthy child and leave them unable to breathe.

That fear lifted in your early childhood. It is one of the first ways the world quietly improved around you.

---

## Within Thirty Days: A Kingdom Changed Hands

*Fourteen days before you were born — February 6, 1952 — King George VI died in his sleep at Sandringham.*

He had been ill with lung cancer for months, but his death still shocked. His daughter Elizabeth, just 25 years old and traveling in Kenya with her husband Philip, learned she had become queen while standing in a treehouse hotel watching elephants. She was four years older than you. She would reign for seventy years — long enough that you would be 70 yourself when she died in September 2022. When you were born, the new queen had been on the throne for two weeks and had not yet been crowned. The world was still adjusting to the word *Queen* after fifteen years of *King*.

---

## The Lifetime Arc

You are 74 years old now, and the span of that life is almost too large to hold in one thought.

You were born before commercial jet passenger service was commonplace, before rock and roll existed as a genre, before television was in most American homes. In the first decade of your life: Sputnik overhead, Elvis on the radio, a new queen crowned in Westminster Abbey. In your teenage years: Kennedy shot, the Beatles arriving in America twelve years after you did, the first humans standing on the moon when you were 17.

You came of age during Vietnam, Watergate, the oil shocks. You watched the Berlin Wall come down at 37, the World Wide Web emerge at 39. You carried a mobile phone before most people owned a computer. You watched two towers fall at 49. You lived through a global pandemic at 68.

And now, at 74, you are living in a moment when machines hold conversations.

---

## What Kind of World

The world you entered in February 1952 had roughly 2.5 billion people, no satellite communications, no commercial computers, no polio vaccine, and a queen who had just taken the throne. The dominant anxieties were nuclear and geopolitical — civilizational, yes, but largely external. Most people in the industrialized world had never seen television in a private home.

What changed during your lifetime was not just technology. It was the pace and texture of change itself. The distance between your birth year and today is not simply 74 years of history. It is several complete eras of human experience, each one reshaping what it meant to communicate, to travel, to be sick, to be informed, to be governed.

You were there for all of it — which is no small thing.
